Model diagnostic support and conventions

Source: R/diagnostic-support.R
diagnostic_support.Rd

Diagnostics use each model's fitted response distribution, observation order and choice of conditioning. The same calculations then produce residuals, reference values and plots across fitting packages.

Details

A conditional check holds fitted random effects fixed. A marginal check averages over their fitted distribution. When responses share random effects or residual correlation, they must be simulated together to preserve that dependence; this is called joint response simulation below. Whether responses are independent depends on the chosen conditioning, not just the model class.

Coverage

PIT means probability integral transform: the fitted cumulative distribution function (CDF) maps each observation to a probability. At discrete values, that probability is randomised over the corresponding probability mass. Quantile residuals transform PIT values to standard-normal scores. Surrogate residuals for mgcv::ocat() models transform the same randomised probabilities to logistic scores. Their reference has location zero and scale one, and fitting weights do not rescale it. They hold fitted random effects fixed and use the same observation alignment and seed conventions. For mgcv::multinom() GAMs, surrogate residuals are vectors of centred Gumbel utility errors, one for every category including 0, following Cheng, Wang and Zhang (2021). Conditional utility draws preserve category identity and are shared across ordinary and scalable panels. Each component has its own QQ/worm reference and pointwise bands; residual panels use that category's fitted probability, and covariate panels separate categories. Select them explicitly with type = "surrogate"; see surrogate_residuals(). A posterior predictive check (PPC) compares observed responses with simulated data sets that also include approximate uncertainty in fitted parameters.

This table applies to the supported response families described below.

  • lm/glm: weighted Gaussian and supported response families, with their fitted dispersion. Quasi families do not specify a response distribution, so they do not support PIT/quantile residuals or PPCs.

  • gam/bam: ordinary, distributional and grouped families, including weighted Gamma, inverse Gaussian, twlss, ordinal and ziP distributions. Multivariate-normal PITs check each response separately; simulations retain covariance between responses. Multinomial PIT/quantile residuals accumulate category probabilities in mgcv's numeric coding order, 0, ..., K. Nominal multinomial GAMs also support utility surrogate residuals in ordinary and scalable plots. Utility residuals need no ordering of categories. Traditional residual checks and PPCs remain available.

  • SCAM models support ordinary posterior predictive plots. Scalable posterior predictive plots are not currently available; use scalable = FALSE. Smoothing-parameter uncertainty is not currently supported for SCAM models; use unconditional = FALSE.

  • gamm/gamm4 and direct lme/merMod fits use their full predictors. Gaussian nlme variance weights and residual covariance are retained. Non-Gaussian gamm fits use penalized quasi-likelihood (PQL). Without residual correlation, these support approximate response checks and PPCs based on their fitted working parameters. PQL residual correlation acts on the working response used for fitting; it does not specify a joint distribution for the observed responses.

  • glmmTMB: conditional Gaussian, Poisson, binomial, NB1/NB2, beta, Gamma, Tweedie, lognormal and supported truncated distributions, including fitted zero inflation and dispersion. Marginal simulations also provide reference samples for other families that glmmTMB can simulate. Unsupported conditional family CDFs remain unavailable. The package's own joint simulator preserves temporal AR1, spatial covariance and correlated random slopes.

  • Univariate GJRM::gamlss: uncensored N, LN, GA, GAi, P, NBI, NBII, BE, LO, WEI, IG, GU and rGU. These include beta, logistic, Weibull, inverse Gaussian and both Gumbel orientations. GAi is accepted by the diagnostic adapter, but some GJRM versions do not offer it in gamlss(). Probabilities use the final likelihood parameters. This corrects stored NBII probabilities that use a Poisson CDF in some upstream versions. Other families and joint, censored and survival models are not yet supported. PIT/quantile, response, Pearson and DHARMa-style residuals are available for all these families. Deviance residuals are available for N, GA, GAi and P only. Quantile QQ plots use method = NULL or "normal"; PIT and DHARMa-style QQ plots require method = NULL. Response and Pearson QQ plots support inverse-CDF ("uniform"), simulated ("simulate"), normal approximation ("normal") and pooled marginal ("marginal") references. Observed-versus-fitted panels use response means, including the Weibull and Gumbel corrections. Residuals are plotted against the first predictor, which controls Weibull scale or logistic/Gumbel location in those families. Posterior predictive checks draw both equations' coefficients together, including beta's logit-linked scale parameter.

  • sdmTMB: supported single-response and delta families retain spatial, spatiotemporal, grouping, time-varying and smooth effects. Standard deltas and deltas with the coupled Poisson link support checks of the complete response, occurrence and positive component. sdmTMB's transformations from internal parameters to response parameters must be available. Student-t checks use the fitted location, scale and fixed or estimated degrees of freedom. Pearson residuals require degrees of freedom above two; PIT/quantile residuals and predictive checks remain available with infinite variance. Predictive plots also support native response families whose analytic residual distributions are unavailable.

Response encodings and residual definitions

Factor-valued binomial responses are Bernoulli observations, even when likelihood weights exceed one. Numeric proportions use the fitted trial counts; paired success/failure counts retain their grouped-binomial encoding. Default response simulations and CDFs follow that distinction. Explicit GAM sampling weights can change trial counts or response precision, including Gaussian AR1 precision, without changing fitted coefficient uncertainty. MASS negative-binomial GLM families use their fitted size parameter. The native gaulss likelihood ignores fitting weights, so its default diagnostic references use the fitted inverse standard deviation directly. Explicit sampling precision weights remain available; see the sampling documentation for how these change the response distribution.

Native beta-regression simulation clips draws at epsilon and one minus epsilon. These endpoints therefore have probability mass. Diagnostics include that mass in their CDFs and randomisation and use moments of the same clipped distribution. This is labelled an approximation: the fitting likelihood evaluates the underlying beta density at epsilon-adjusted observations. Distribution functions supplied by callers are preserved.

GEV and sinh-arcsinh checks use stable response means and correct residual centering and signs for both observed and simulated responses. Their deviance magnitudes follow the fitting package's definitions: GEV uses the square root of its saturated log-likelihood contrast; sinh-arcsinh uses zero log density as its reference. If a sinh-arcsinh density exceeds one, that contrast is negative. Deviance checks then give an error rather than replace the residual with zero; response and PIT/quantile checks remain available. These deviance definitions do not produce comparable standardised scores across families. Use PIT/quantile residuals for uniform/standard-normal references.

GEV means and variances require shape below one and one-half, respectively. Signed deviance checks also require a finite mean and shape at least minus one. PIT/quantile checks do not require these moments. When the response mean does not exist, appraisal explains why the observed-versus-fitted panel is unavailable and retains the PIT/quantile panels.

nlme calculations retain covariance between random effects, including nested groups and block designs. They also retain the contrasts and observation order used for fitting, including after subsetting or missing-value removal. Changing global contrast options after fitting does not change the diagnostics.

Conditioning and dependence

For response references, conditioning = "conditional" usually holds fitted random effects and nuisance parameters fixed. "marginal" simulates new effects from their fitted distributions and averages over them. Setting random effects to zero is not a substitute for this averaging, especially with nonlinear response links. sdmTMB has additional field choices described below. PPCs separately include approximate uncertainty in fitted parameters.

"gam_component" explicitly uses the extracted GAM component. gamm and gamm4 diagnostics and posterior predictive checks default to the full model with conditional conditioning. gamm4 response simulations use the same default; the existing gamm response simulator retains its GAM-component default. Conditional response references hold fitted effects fixed, while conditional PPCs include uncertainty in those fitted effects. Specify "marginal" to simulate new effects instead.

Conditional glmmTMB/lme4 response likelihoods factorize given all random effects, including temporal and spatial effects. Marginal responses may be dependent because they share those effects. An independent effect for each observation need not create dependence between observations. The calculations check covariance implied by the fitted random-effect design, including correlated slopes and covariance cancellation. Gaussian nlme residual correlation can remain after conditioning on random effects; variance weights alone do not introduce correlation.

A conditional check at estimated effects assesses the response distribution at those estimates. It does not provide a calibrated test of random-effect covariance or of the whole fitted model. Marginal joint references assess response variation implied by new simulated effects. A QQ plot checks the distribution of residuals; inspect their ordering or spatial pattern as well to assess dependence. Models are not refitted when calculating reference bands.

BAM working correlation

Gaussian identity-link AR1 BAM retains joint response simulation, with new independent series starting at AR.start boundaries. For non-Gaussian or nonidentity models fitted with discrete = TRUE and nonzero rho, BAM applies AR1 to working residuals as a generalized estimating equations (GEE) approximation. This does not specify a unique joint response distribution. The restriction applies to supported extended.family and GLM families. See https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/mgcv/html/bam.html.

Fitted marginal CDFs, inverse CDFs and PIT/quantile residuals remain useful. For traditional residuals, the default QQ plot and a requested inverse-CDF QQ plot use method = "marginal". This approximates the pooled distribution of individual residuals by numerical sampling, without asserting independence or supplying dependence bands. Explicit method = "simulate", joint response simulation and PPCs give an explanatory error. No additional dependence model, such as a copula, is introduced. An explicitly requested "normal" approximation is available without independence-based bands; it is never the default here.

residual_correlation() and residual_correlation_plot() provide approximate checks of correlation between residuals at different lags. For non-Gaussian BAM, the stored std.rsd residuals differ from the weighted working residuals used in fitting. Adjusting working residuals for the fitted AR1 correlation (whitening) or using std.rsd can reveal remaining serial structure. Neither supplies a generative response model or calibrated p-values. Series boundaries and gaps from missing observations are retained, and no significance bands based on independence are drawn. Lags count observation positions, not spatial distance or irregular elapsed time. Specify series and order the fitting data to suit the dependence being checked.

sdmTMB field choices

With fixed-effect coefficients and covariance parameters held at their maximum likelihood estimates (MLEs):

  • field_method = "mle-mvn" (default) follows sdmTMB's recommended approach: draw the fitted fields together from their approximate posterior distribution, then hold that draw fixed for conditional PITs and response references. Response errors are independent given those fields. Reference bands use the same draw as the observed residuals.

  • "mle-eb" holds empirical-Bayes field estimates fixed. This matches sdmTMB's residual construction at fitted fields, which its documentation does not recommend for goodness-of-fit testing. Shrinkage and estimation can distort the resulting residual distribution.

  • "mle-mvn-integrated" averages over approximate uncertainty in fitted fields using sdmTMB's joint response simulations. Residuals are calculated from ranks in these simulations rather than from one fixed draw of fields. This reuses the fitting data and can give conservative checks; treat the results as approximate posterior predictive checks.

  • conditioning = "marginal" instead simulates new spatial, spatiotemporal and grouping effects. Simulation at fitting observations also renews other supported field and time-varying effects; smooths remain fitted. field_method does not cause another field draw in this mode.

gratia.diagnostics.field_seed (default 1) makes the posterior field draw reproducible independently of PIT randomisation. All panels use the same draw. To inspect further draws, change this option and present the results together. The sdmTMB definitions and recommendations are documented at https://sdmtmb.github.io/sdmTMB/reference/residuals.sdmTMB.html and https://sdmtmb.github.io/sdmTMB/articles/residual-checking.html.

PPCs use a separate approximation that draws fixed-effect, nuisance and field parameters together. Marginal PPCs simulate new fields at each parameter draw; smooths retain their posterior draws. Plot captions identify conditioning. Parameter estimation, the Gaussian approximation to the posterior and finite simulation error affect these checks. None of these modes guarantees that goodness-of-fit tests attain their nominal false-positive rate after fitting.

Calculating reference values and bands

Analytic PIT/quantile QQ plots use uniform/standard-normal reference quantiles. For ideal independent responses, bands are pointwise intervals for ordered residuals. For dependent responses, bands come from joint simulations (n_simulate) when a joint generator exists. Otherwise the bands are omitted and the plot explains why. Bands condition on the chosen fitted distribution and fields. They do not provide simultaneous coverage or account for refitting.

When a joint simulator is available but marginal CDFs or moments cannot be calculated analytically, one reference sample of simulated data sets supplies means, variances and residual ranks. With R reference draws, PIT is (number below + U * (ties + 1))/(R + 1), where U is uniform on (0, 1). The extra rank position is for the observation being checked, which keeps normal scores finite even outside the simulated range. Observed and simulated responses use the same reference sample, centering and residual definitions. These ranks need not equal the empirical CDF at an observation.

options(gratia.diagnostics.marginal_draws = 249L) sets the reference sample size (minimum 19). Increase it to assess sensitivity to Monte Carlo error. gratia.diagnostics.marginal_seed (default 1) makes this sample reproducible independently of residual randomisation. A finite sample limits tail resolution and moment accuracy. Moment estimates require finite population moments: glmmTMB Student-t response residuals require df > 1, and Pearson residuals require df > 2. An undefined moment is not replaced by a finite sample estimate. PIT/quantile checks and joint draws remain available, but an undefined mean cannot be shown as a fitted expectation. Bands for residuals calculated from simulation ranks use joint draws and the same rank transformation, even if the underlying responses are independent. Marginal deviance residuals remain unavailable where the integrated likelihood has no defined deviance; use response, Pearson or quantile residuals instead.

DHARMa-style residuals

dharma_residuals() and type = "dharma" implement simulation-based PIT residuals using gratia's existing generators, without requiring DHARMa or mgcViz. Responses are ranked against n_dharma simulated datasets (default 250), with randomisation within ties and exact zero and one endpoints. This calculation differs from the existing simulation-rank formula above: it uses the empirical fractions below and below or equal to the observation, without an extra rank position. Existing PIT and quantile residuals retain their current definitions.

The calculation needs comparable scalar response draws, but no CDF or finite response moments. Existing model adapters retain their conditioning defaults. Marginal-only generators provide marginal distribution checks. Censored and multivariate observations are unsupported. Independent responses use uniform QQ references with approximate pointwise bands because the simulation count is finite; dependent responses omit independence-based bands.

Remaining limitations and extensions

Inverse CDFs with direct lower/upper and log-probability arguments preserve extreme interior quantiles. Older functions that accept only lower-tail probabilities cannot always represent an extreme upper-tail probability. If conversion rounds it to an endpoint and produces a false infinite quantile, an explanatory error is raised. This limits extreme upper quantiles of the compound-Poisson Tweedie distribution. The Gamma boundary and inverse-Gaussian solver accept log probabilities directly. True probability endpoints remain valid.

BAM/PQL working correlations need a scientifically specified joint response model before joint simulation or PPC can be added. Additional GJRM and other fitting-package families should supply their parameters to the shared response distributions. Censored/survival PPCs need a way to reapply censoring to each simulated response. Nominal multivariate PITs need a documented category ordering or a different multivariate diagnostic. Unrecognised random-effect structures remain unsupported. Diagnostics do not repair na.pass fits where missing responses cannot be aligned with predictions and residuals; ordinary na.omit/na.exclude fits are covered. MCMC, model refitting and calibrated dependence tests would require additional sampling or refitting methods.

Large data sets and family functions

Like mgcViz, these diagnostics use residuals with known reference distributions where available and aggregate large data sets before plotting. All observations and QQ endpoints contribute. Kernel density estimates and histograms remain available as separate views. See https://mfasiolo.github.io/mgcViz/reference/qq.gamViz.html. mgcViz approximates QQ plots on a discrete grid; gratia aggregates plot points but preserves exact pooled reference quantiles. mgcViz also plots differences between empirical and model-implied conditional densities. Adding such plots would require comparable smoothing bandwidths and a validated conditional reference. The existing density and histogram views retain information about scale misspecification rather than rescaling every residual to unit variance. See https://mfasiolo.github.io/mgcViz/reference/l_densCheck.html.

Uniform references average ordered residuals as draws are generated, without storing all draws. Simulated QQ uses exact pooled quantiles computed as by stats::quantile(type = 7) and pointwise intervals for each residual rank. Above options(gratia.diagnostics.max_cells = 1e7), sorted draws are written to temporary files and merged exactly. This limits simulation memory use at the cost of disk I/O. One response vector and the reference output must still fit in memory. Scalable PPCs summarise every draw on the same grid; discrete responses with more than 512 distinct values use labelled probabilities for 512 bins. posterior_samples() returns the raw response draws. Coefficient and random-effect draws still need memory proportional to the number of parameters times the number of draws.

The internal fix_family_rd(), fix_family_cdf() and fix_family_qf() functions still add $rd, $cdf and $qf to mgcv-compatible families while preserving functions supplied by callers. The fitted-distribution code adapts their arguments locally. Families can supply a gratia_diagnostics function for response moments, probability bounds and other distribution information; see family_diagnostics for the interface. Other fitting packages can use the same standard response distributions, or combine them by family index, truncate them or add point masses without changing the plotting calculations.
